newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew face risky DIY repairs in space.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew face risky DIY repairs in space.

text.p: They are a Russian air force pilot, a Russian rocket scientist and an egghead astrophysicist from England. Now they have just over a week to turn themselves into the best do-it-yourself electricians in the solar system.

The three-man crew of Russia's crippled Mir space station face a complex and dangerous job to patch up their electricity supply after the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history. Vital tools will arrive by unmanned cargo craft in 10 days or so.
The task facing commander Vasily Tsibliyev, his flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin and British-born American physicist Michael Foale sounds simple.
They must reconnect 22 cables from solar panels that should provide a third of Mir's electricity but which were detached when the crew sealed one of its modules after the accident.

What makes a mundane bit of household DIY into a high-stakes task of cosmic surgery is having to do it in bulky space suits inside the damaged module and then feed the cables back into the main part of the station without letting Mir's fragile air supply escape in the opposite direction.
"It will be a very complicated operation," Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev warned on Friday.

When the 7.5-tonne Progress M-34 freighter rammed into the Spektr scientific module on Wednesday during a training manoeuvre -- it is not clear if the pilot, Tsibliyev, or the machine was at fault -- it smashed one of four solar panels on the module.
But most importantly it poked a small hole in the two-year-old Spektr's hull, sending air hissing out into space.

Only split-second reactions allowed the crew to slam shut two airtight doors separating Spektr, saving Mir's other modules and themselves from the fate of three Soviet cosmonauts who suffocated on Soyuz 11 in 1971 when a pressure valve broke.
Now the trick is to go back into Spektr, hitch up the cables from the three undamaged solar panels and connect them back into the station without leaving cracks in the oxygen seal.
The key to this operation is being manufactured against the clock by the Energiya factory near Moscow this weekend.
Known as a "hermoplate", it is a plaque to be fitted on to one of the airlock doors. It holds 22 hermetic valves that will let the power cables be fed through without letting air escape.
The Zvezda (Star) factory will need several days to produce special adapters for Tsibliyev and Lazutkin's space suits, to allow them to work inside the Spektr module.
Before they get to work, the cosmonauts also face problems simply docking with the unmanned Progress M-35 which is due to blast off with their repair supplies on July 4 or 5.
Mir's reduced power will make the operation "very difficult" Russian officials say, raising the possibility of a space walk to retrieve the tools.

Working in the cramped confines of the Spektr, where much of Mir's scientific equipment -- and Michael Foale's toothbrush -- are stranded, will be extremely awkward in bulky spacesuits. Access to the module is only 80 cm (31 inches) wide.

As a measure of the risks during the rewiring operation, Mission Control told NASA scientist Foale he will sit in Mir's lone Soyuz escape capsule while the Russian Mir experts work to be ready for a quick getaway if something goes wrong.
As one of the weary Russians told Mission Control on Friday when the job was explained: "It's very problematic."
